review:
The Metronomicon: Slay The Dance Floor is one of the more inventive genre hybrids released in recent years, combining rhythm-based gameplay with role-playing mechanics in a way that feels surprisingly natural. Developed by Puuba and published by Akupara Games, the title takes the familiar structure of a fantasy RPG and reimagines it through the lens of a music game. Instead of selecting commands from menus or waiting for turns to unfold, players must perform actions in time with a constantly evolving soundtrack. The result is a fast-paced adventure that demands both strategic thinking and rhythmic precision, creating an experience unlike most traditional RPGs or rhythm games.

The game's story embraces a playful and deliberately absurd premise. Strange dance parties have begun appearing across the world, attracting dangerous monsters and spreading chaos wherever they emerge. To stop this unusual threat, a group of heroes trained at a specialized academy must travel across various regions, confront increasingly powerful enemies, and uncover the source of the mysterious musical invasion. The narrative never takes itself too seriously, relying instead on humor, colorful characters, and a lighthearted tone that complements the game's energetic nature.

What truly sets The Metronomicon apart is its combat system. Battles unfold through multiple rhythm lanes that correspond to different party members. As notes scroll across the screen, players must hit them accurately to generate attacks, cast spells, activate support abilities, and defend against incoming threats. Unlike most rhythm games, however, maintaining perfect timing is only part of the challenge. Players must also monitor their entire party, switch focus between heroes, and decide which abilities should be used at specific moments. This creates a unique blend of multitasking and strategy that keeps encounters exciting from beginning to end.

The role-playing mechanics are integrated remarkably well into the musical framework. Characters gain experience, improve their abilities, and acquire equipment that alters their effectiveness during battle. Different heroes fulfill specific roles within the party, encouraging players to think carefully about team composition. Some characters specialize in dealing damage, while others focus on healing, buffs, debuffs, or defensive support. As the adventure progresses, managing the party becomes increasingly important, adding genuine depth beyond simply hitting notes accurately.

One of the strongest aspects of the game is its soundtrack. The developers assembled an impressive collection of licensed songs from various artists spanning electronic, indie, synth-pop, and dance-inspired genres. Each track feels distinct, introducing unique rhythm patterns and combat challenges that keep gameplay fresh throughout the campaign. The music is not merely background entertainment; it is the driving force behind every mechanic in the game. Because battles are built around individual songs, the soundtrack becomes inseparable from the overall experience and plays a crucial role in maintaining engagement.

The visual design matches the energy of the music exceptionally well. Character models are expressive, enemy designs are imaginative, and environments are packed with colorful details. Every battle feels lively and animated, creating a spectacle that complements the constant movement of the rhythm lanes. The fantasy setting allows for a wide variety of locations and creatures, ensuring that players encounter something visually interesting throughout the adventure. The presentation successfully balances readability and style, allowing players to focus on gameplay without sacrificing visual appeal.

Another notable strength is the amount of content available. Beyond the main campaign, players can participate in challenge modes, side missions, endless gameplay options, and various replayable activities. The Slay The Dance Floor edition expanded the original release considerably by introducing new characters, additional abilities, cooperative play, and extra game modes. These additions significantly increase replay value and provide incentives for players who want to master every aspect of the combat system.

The cooperative multiplayer mode deserves particular praise. Few rhythm games successfully implement cooperative play, yet The Metronomicon manages to make it feel both functional and entertaining. Sharing responsibility for managing the party while maintaining rhythm adds a fresh dimension to the experience. Playing alongside a friend can transform already chaotic battles into memorable and highly enjoyable sessions, making co-op one of the game's standout features.

Accessibility is another area where the game performs well. Difficulty options and adjustable settings allow newcomers to enjoy the adventure without becoming overwhelmed. At the same time, higher difficulty levels provide a substantial challenge for experienced rhythm game enthusiasts. This flexibility broadens the game's appeal and ensures that both casual and dedicated players can find an appropriate level of challenge.

The game's few weaknesses stem primarily from the complexity of its hybrid design. New players may initially struggle to balance rhythm inputs with party management responsibilities, especially during more demanding encounters. Some sections can feel overwhelming until the mechanics become second nature. Additionally, players seeking a deeply narrative-driven RPG may find the story secondary to the gameplay systems. However, these issues rarely overshadow the overall quality of the experience.

Ultimately, The Metronomicon: Slay The Dance Floor succeeds because it fully embraces its unconventional concept. Rather than simply adding musical elements to an RPG or RPG elements to a rhythm game, it creates a genuine fusion where both genres support one another. Every battle requires equal parts musical skill and strategic planning, resulting in gameplay that remains engaging long after the initial novelty has faded.

For players looking for something different from traditional role-playing adventures or standard rhythm games, The Metronomicon offers a refreshingly original experience. Its memorable soundtrack, creative combat mechanics, charming presentation, and substantial amount of content make it one of the most distinctive titles in either genre. It may not appeal to everyone, but those willing to embrace its unusual design will discover a highly entertaining and surprisingly deep adventure.

Rating: 8/10

The Metronomicon: Slay The Dance Floor è un gioco che fonde alla perfezione il ritmo musicale con elementi RPG, offrendo un gameplay avvincente e assolutamente irresistibile.
Il gioco consiste nel sconfiggere i nemici a ritmo di musica, "passando" da un eroe all’altro per scatenare attacchi, magie e abilità speciali. Il comparto musicale è straordinario: The Metronomicon vanta una tracklist variegata, con brani memorabili che ti restano in testa anche dopo aver smesso di giocare. Un altro punto forte è il sistema di progressione: ogni eroe ha un set unico di abilità che puoi personalizzare e combinare con quelle degli altri membri del team, creando una sinergia perfetta in battaglia anche tramite i potenti oggetti che puoi acquistare con la valuta di gioco. Anche il design visivo, con colori vivaci, uno stile cartoonesco e animazioni esilaranti rende l’esperienza ancora più accattivante.
Il gioco offre tre livelli di difficoltà: Facile, Medio e Difficile. La scelta della difficoltà influisce solo sul numero di note che compariranno a schermo, senza modificare i danni subiti. Questo significa che, se non si dispone di un team con un alto DPS, per una sfida immediata è possibile impostare sin da subito il livello più alto. A proposito di sfide, The Metronomicon propone una vasta gamma di modalità, come "L'arena", dove si devono superare determinate prove con personaggi predefiniti, o la modalità "Infinita", in cui, dopo ogni canzone superata, il gioco aggiunge un malus.
The Metronomicon: Slay The Dance Floor è una perla rara nel mondo dei videogiochi. È creativo, divertente e capace di sorprendere costantemente. Riesce a combinare due generi apparentemente lontani in modo perfetto, senza sacrificare né la profondità del gameplay né il puro divertimento.
Lo consiglio a chiunque ami i giochi ritmici, gli RPG o semplicemente a chi vuole provare qualcosa di davvero innovativo e coinvolgente. In poche parole, è un titolo imperdibile.
Voto: 10/10

Alright. I had a long-ass review before. I'm gonna simplify now.

If you've played the following games, you'll probably understand what I mean when I say it's Amplitude or Frequency from the PS2 era, but contextualized as a party-focused RPG.

If you haven't played them, it's just Dance Dance Revolution (or StepMania, Pump It Up, etc.) with lane switching.

If you don't care about rhythm games, think of it this way:
Do you about know the stratagems from Helldivers? It's that mechanic but it's a rhythm game. You have 12 stratagems total, split up in 4 options (lanes, or the characters in your party), where you get to the higher tiers of those options (up to 3) by keeping the rhythm going for longer. You can get some pretty broken combos going with a lot of different character and gear setups, which helps break up some of the monotony of replaying charts in rhythm games.

[b] The Metronomicon: Slay the Dance Floor [/b] is a neat little rhythm gem that is definitively worth a try, at the very least during a sale.

I have gone through the game using a keyboard (DFJK, with S and L for character swapping). While I cannot comment on the controller functionality (and the issues brought up by other users) I can say the game plays very nicely on keyboard, with only a bit of time needed to get used to the swapping mechanics. After a few hours, quickly selecting different characters in order to cast abilities and avoiding danger becomes second nature.

Song selection in the base game is quite enjoyable, though this point is rather subjective. Objectively, they fit the game's aesthetic very well and they compliment the resulting note charts nicely. 

Speaking of charts, the songs are fun to play; each lane has different charting, with note density varying throughout the songs making sure each lane has its easier and harder moments. This meshes together well with the combat aspect of the game. As enemies wittle down your hp and debuffs start flying, you may find yourself needing to adapt on the fly, which avoids a common RPG issue of complacent strategies.

The RPG systems service the game well. It's robust enough to have some depth without becoming overwhelming. I enjoyed the characters' skill selection and found myself changing up my party's composition very often. I never felt like a character or build was overpowering every other options.

I also really enjoyed the Arena unlocked early on in the campaign. This section opens up challenges with pre-built teams. These required me to think more about the RPG aspects of the game to understand the strategy I needed to use with the team I was given for a challenge. It also doubles as a sort of tutorial for certain tactics or characters the player may not have been using at the time, or how to kill a certain type or enemy, which could then be used during the story.

Progression through the campaign is straightforward, but can be a little iffy at times depending on your experience. I went through most of the solo campaign in hard mode without issue, but hit a wall during the final area where enemies were bringing my hp down faster than I could recover it. It kind of dampened the feeling I had where I could get through anything if I didn't miss notes and picked a good team for the level. Thankfully, the grind to bring my team up to speed was short and didn't feel aimless, as there is plenty of secrets (like defeating each songs' minibosses) to give the player a goal while grinding.

Some information is also difficult to understand at first without a bit of searching, which makes the game a bit harder to get into if you're not already sold on the concept. The UI is a bit scattered, which makes keeping track of things like song progression and enemy information like buffs and elements a bit difficult since your eyes will usually be focused on your gameplay area (ie. the notes).

Overall, Metronomicon is a good experience for a niche of players who like rhythm games and are willing to give a funky concept a try.

Even though The Metronomicon: Slay the Dance Floor is a few years old, I bought it recently after it was featured in the Save&Sound Indie Music Festival.  While this game definitely has its flaws, it is overall among the best rhythm-type games I have played on Steam to date, and might be worth picking up if you are after that type of experience.  

This game is a hybrid RPG-rhythm mashup, but the rhythm aspect outshines the RPG.  The rhythm portion of the game is exactly along the lines of games such as Stepmania, Dance Dance Revolution, or Flash Flash Revolution - a series of arrows fall from the sky, and you must copy them in rhythm.  Several input modes are supported, including a controller, but my preference is the arrow keys.  Including the DLC, the game features roughly 60 tracks, each playable at 3 difficulty levels.  Overall, the soundtrack is decent, with no really bad songs, though several of them aren't quite my cup of tea. For the most part, the music serves as a pleasantly generic backdrop for the dancing - with a handful of standouts I quite like from the artists Christopher Hoag, Viking Machine, Demoscene Time Machine, and YACHT.  The core rhythm experience is quite good, with well-designed and finely timed step charts and responsive but forgiving input detection.

The other half of the game is the role-playing portion.  There's not much of a story to speak of, but there's a lot of cartoonish and juvenile humor, and the jist is that we are following several recent dance school graduates as they use their new magic dance powers to stop rampaging groups of evil dancing fantasy monsters.  Each song is a battle where you face off against a string of endless enemies, and you have to stay alive while also killing enough of them quickly enough to prevent yourself from becoming overwhelmed.  Enemies can also trip you up by hitting you with statuses that make your arrows fade, spin, or swerve.  You have four characters in battle, 8 unlockable in all,  and each character is equipped with several spells or abilities.  Successfully stringing together some steps will allow your character to attack - the more steps you string together, the higher tier of a spell they will cast. You will have to swap frequently to manage cooldowns, stuns, healing, and support, and there's also final fantasy-esque elemental strengths and weaknesses to worry about.  Your characters will level up, but there is level scaling, so leveling up does feel rather pointless even though it does give you a *slight* edge.

I am having a good time overall with the game, but I do have some complaints.  The step chart is very readable on easy and medium, but the hard difficulty is so dense that it feels slightly too small to be easily readable.  The rest of the battle screen is poorly laid out, as well, with animations sometimes distracting from or blocking the step charts, or with necessary information located in spots that you cannot see out of the corner of your eye when trying to maintain a streak.  Some of the accessories are broken, or don't stack when they should.  Finally, and this is a warning especially to completionists, a ton of the game's content is tied to ridiculous challenge modes (and also requires every single song to be beaten on hard - good luck!).  An "arena" mode requires you to accomplish unique objectives using premade, modifiable teams, some of which are extremely challenging.  An "endless" mode requires you to complete 30 straight songs while also dealing with an increasing number of random penalties.  A "no pee breaks" achievement requires completing a 3.5 hr 50-song playlist back to back without pausing once, which is ideal for those with kids or pets or jobs.

It's flawed and it took me a while to get into the mechanics. I'm still not entirely sure how the character's stats affect the moves and abilities, and the elemental effectiveness was a bit hard to keep track on during the actual fights for me.
But it has some seriously great ideas of how to pair RPG elements with rhythm game elements. The way you can switch out the character's moves and decide on the sequence, so you can strategically decide to hit more consecutive notes or less depending on which move you want to perform, is pretty clever. Switching through the 4 characters and their respective rhythm sheets on a whim during the fights works better than I expected it to and if you get into a flow, it's very satisfying. It can be exhausting, but it's mostly in a good way.

Some songs were a bit frustrating for me but thankfully it lets you adjust the difficulty level for each individual song and you don't actually have to beat every single one to progress in the story. I had to play 3 of the songs in easy mode throughout the campaign because a few of the beat maps had some really hard spots here and there that I kept dying at.

The music is very hit and miss for me when it comes to their sound. There were some songs that I genuinely liked, and I was pretty excited when I saw that a song by Jimmy Urine from Mindless Self Indulgence was one of the boss fights, but some of the songs were just obnoxious to me. That didn't really hinder the enjoyment much, because even the songs I didn't like had some fun beat mappings for the most part.

The game also has some very nice visual design at points. Although the story cutscenes look a bit flat, the animated in-game environments and creatures were really nice to look at. Only problem is that you never really get to look at those because you're so focused on hitting the beats. lol

I wouldn't call this game amazing, but I would be very down to playing a sequel with some possible improvements and new features. The core concept is pretty great and the execution is solid.

In many more words, Metronomicon is, as advertised, a mix of rythm and rpg, and boy has it been executed well. It's honestly amazing.
First of all, despite this game being an indie title developed by a small studio that simply doesn't have the money to license big, well known songs, the song's library of 50+ songs seriously won't disappoint you. Just like the game, the songs in it are hidden gems in themselves. All of them are absolute bops and perfectly set the mood.
The gameplay differs from other rythm games out there like Stepmania, as instead of having just one track with 4 lanes, you have 4. That being said, you only ever play on one, currently active track, so it doesn't get too overwhelming, and in fact acts as a nice change of pace. Instead of focusing only on playing the track well, you need to also think on which track you want to play based on the abilities you currently need the most, the amount of notes on that track, etc.
Now, to explain why this is so important, I need to quickly go over how hero customisation, another great part of the game, works. Each hero has 6 primary abilities, as well as 2 secondary abilities to choose from. You may only have 3 primaries and 1 secondary selected at a time, however, you can pick the order in which your primaries are set in. The reason why this is important is that the way you cycle between abilities is by playing the track for specific amounts of time. Essentially, as you play, you reach checkpoints, which in turn will queue your ability. Now, if you either miss or switch off of the track, the hero will cast that ability, however if you reach the next champion, it is replaced by next ability in order. The later the ability is in the order, the stronger it will be, which adds this extra layer of thinking, where you gotta consider if you want a specific ability to be a quick cast for small benefit, or maybe a lvl 3 with a powerful effect. This combined with the total of 9 heroes allows for great variety when it comes to how you build your party.
Now, that means that, in total, when playing a song, you'll not only focus on which buttons to press, but also:
-Which hero do I switch to?
-Which ability do I use? Do I just go for the quickie, or do I try to go for the next one in order?
-How much health do I/the enemy have?
-Are all of my buffs up? If no, do I need to reapply them?
All of this makes Metronomicon's gameplay incredibly dynamic.
Additionally, this game has support for Stepmania song files, which means you can enjoy your favourite custom songs made for that game in here!
That being said, this game does have a few, minor flaws.
-To unlock anything in freeplay, you will have to first unlock it in the story mode, so you  can't exactly skip the grind.
-Sometimes, your heroes will simply not be at a high enough level to take on more difficult enemies, such as bosses, leading to progression walls that you have to grind to overpass.
-The game does have slight RNG aspects to it. They are few and far between, but can make your gameplay that tad bit less enjoyable.
-The story is... eh...

All that being said though, The Metronomicon: Slay The Dance Floor, is a fantastic game that is absolutely worth your time. If you like rythm games, buy it. If you don't usually enjoy rythm games, buy it when it's on sale. You probably won't regret it.

There's a lot to say about this game. Not necessarily negative or positive though I have a tendency to phrase things in a negative tone. It goes one sale pretty cheap so I'll give it a yes.

The game itself looked like an interesting blend, and it is for some. I personally enjoyed using rhythm matching to cast spells. It does it fairly well in my opinion. You use two buttons to swap between characters, then match as many presses as needed to cast. The background of the runway changes to indicate which spell you're working towards. If you want to cast the first skill you go till you hit the bright arrows and the color changes and then switch characters or intentionally miss. If you continue on you'll cast the 2nd spell if you get far enough and then the 3rd. Importantly, it doesn't count as a failed press until you've hit a button, so after switching characters you can wait for a good part to start pressing. Status can make things harder by causing arrows to wiggle, spin, lose color, etc. Most of your actions outside of casting comes from party builds. You start with 4 characters and pick up 4 more as you go. each character has 2 item slots, there are 4 stats. you can equip 3 spells and 1 passive spell. Though in total there are only about 5-6 spells per person to chose from. And some characters are stuck in their rolls, the medic only gets 1 damage spell and it's late game, the caster gets no real support. There are 5 areas you go through and each one has about 8-10 songs some turning into challenges. There is also a multiplayer mode where each person can control a lane allowing two casts at once, which works pretty well I'd say, that's how I played the entire game. 

That all said the songs aren't really that varied, or that great in my opinion. I doubt you'll recognize many if any of them and they're almost all edm with maybe 1 rock/metal song per area. The animations in the game aren't great either, they look like a flash game really. The biggest complaint I'd say I have is that there's way too much to pay attention to. Some attacks hit multiple enemies, but I couldn't really tell when there were multiple enemies on screen. The buff bar is under each character and hard to catch while looking at the notes. Each enemy has an attunement that dictates their weakness (Fire is weak to water attacks etc...) but it's above their health bar on the right side of the screen. The streak meter on the top right is accompanied by a bar in challenges to show how close you are to completing it and the time remaining in the song. Also, every character has their own health but it seems all condensed into one big party health bar on the left side. In the end we ended up using Gruver the druid because he had a skill that refreshes all the buffs. Spamming that let us ingore that mechanic mostly as it would maintain taunt, haste, and focus making damage predictable, cooldowns short, and make casting faster.

Before I go on, I should probably speak towards my short time playing this game on Steam:
The controller support was finicky and so I purchased the game a second time on PS4. I should note that it's become more and more apparent as I've played higher difficulty songs that the note tracks are designed with PC in mind and are much, much harder to handle on a dpad controller. In an ironic turn of fate, Metronomicon has the same issue many Japanese rhythm games have; higher difficulties are nigh-impossible without using the intended hardware, be it arcade stick or keyboard, as the porting to use of a controller was an afterthought.  Regardless, I've since played through the game on PS4 with a Dualshock 4 controller and, while I enjoyed my time with it, I find it unlikely many other people will unless they share my patience bordering on masochistic tenacity.

Metronomicon tries to be both an RPG and a Rhythm game. Marrying these genres proves to be a shaky union and because of that, it's very hard for me to recommend this game to anyone else. What's exactly at odds here?

On the RPG side, there's a general non-specificity when it comes to just about everything in the game. How big of a difference is minor damage from major and major from crazy? How long should I expect these buffs to last? How significant of a difference does it make to overcharge abilities by inputting more notes before executing them? While you're constantly asking yourself questions like this, you're treated to randomly gathered items and it's unclear if loot is tied to specific stages or enemies or bosses and, some times, it's even unclear exactly what that loot does. The combination lifepools into a team health pool works well until you start questioning exactly how healing, percent health triggers, and other effects relate to it all. Ultimately, Metronomicon makes the mistake of giving the player too little information, which, in turn, makes it hard to feel as though you're properly interacting with the systems that are in place. The systems to progress and upgrade your team feel largely outside your agency as a player and 'grinding' songs for experience is a process that doesn't feel all that great and it's unclear how hard difficulty scales to your party levels and what they even do beyond netting you new moves.

At the end of the day, though, the rhythm stuff holds it back--did you want to execute that move of yours? Hope you can hit those notes right. Were you hoping for more direct control of your party? Good luck, you're bound to the frets. Did you want to pause to take in more information and inform your next decision? Too bad; that resets the song track entirely, making you waste precious seconds of the song run time. You'll constantly find yourself unable to make decisions that feel informed because the game is forever ticking down the amount of time left on the song you've got, notes forever whizzing by as a reminder you should, optimally, always be slapping in inputs. Remember--your goal is not to actually beat any bosses; it's just to survive to the end of the song. Metronomicon constantly reminds you that it's a rhythm game first and foremost.

But what about the rhythm game? Honestly, the RPG stuff holds it back. In any other rhythm game, the note sequences would feel absolutely tailored to the songs, but here they're variable based on the character you're using (arbitrarily so, it seems?). Do you like feeling like you're 'in the zone' when playing a rhythm game? Enjoy constantly having to pull out to play this left-brain right-brain exercise of swapping between characters to heal, buff, cleanse debuffs, and deal damage. Were you a fan of being able to focus on the notes in a rhythm game? Metronomicon makes sure all the relevant information you need is at your periphery no matter what--enemy health and type is on the far right while your team health is far left while buffs active are in tiny icons beneath characters while individual character health is something apparently only I care about. This gets to some of the worst offenders, though--debuffs and boss effects. Some debuffs are laughably minimal, such as your icons losing color, whereas others, like the one that waves them around such that it's very difficult to tell if a note is a double note or two notes close together, is a much more frustrating beast. Bosses will mess with your notes as well in ways that aren't always properly telegraphed as even being boss moves; it took me several attempts to realize that the second boss was actually using a move that caused these boulders to fall down, obscure my notes, and hurt my characters and that I had to switch characters to avoid that damage, throwing a huge wrench in the whole 'playing a rhythm game' aspect of things. Sometimes, a boss will use a move that forces you to hit notes or take damage for several seconds, which, in turn, wastes your own time that you need to use to deal damage, which can cost you the fight. It'd be fine if the boss fights were designed around this, but it feels wholly up to RNG when these moves get used. Regardless, you'll constantly find yourself interrupting the flow of rhythm-based play to consider some element of the RPG based play and it's not a great time. Speaking of, missing notes doesn't just interrupt or stop your momentum towards taking an action--it also hurts your party. Fumbling a set of notes can be far more damaging than enemy attacks. If that's not enough, the characters groan and pout every time it happens and there's no option, as far as I can find, that turns this off. Speaking of distractions, various characters will appear and start dancing on screen at random times and this can obscure your characters in a way that's so distracting on top of everything else that it's hard to keep focus on the rhythm game at hand. It's a mess. Left and right note differentiation is fine, but up and down still give me issue even at the end of the game--which wouldn't be as much a problem if hitting the wrong note didn't interrupt my attack or cause me to use the entirely wrong one. Several combo notes require you to suddenly rely on a second set of inputs (wasd if you're using a keyboard, face buttons on a controller) and this strikes me as a strange design decision and something that works far better on the dualshock than it does a keyboard or XBOX controller. Song difficulty varies so wildly that some songs within the same chapter are harder to beat than their boss counterparts. The song list varies from forgettable to a few real bangers and it's a shame more time wasn't spent polishing this end of the game.

While I could gripe on about elements of the art, aesthetic, animation, and plot, those are all minor points to what I've outlined so far. Metronomicon is a flawed game. There's nothing else quite like it, and if you're like me, you'll play and enjoy it despite the flaws, shortcomings, and frustrations, but for the general person looking to pick up a game? Maybe the adventure you're looking for is at a different dance hall.
